usedCounterFrames: thinking-fast-and-slow-ch01: The mistake is not having a fast first impression. The mistake is letting that impression wear the badge of a checked judgment before System 2 has done any deliberate checking.

thinking-fast-and-slow-ch02: The risky move is treating attention as character. It is a limited capacity, so the better move is to notice when a judgment needs mental work before a fluent answer gets trusted.
thinking-fast-and-slow-ch03: The lazy controller is not stupidity. It is effort avoidance inside a capable mind, where System 2 accepts a convenient answer because monitoring would cost more work.

thinking-fast-and-slow-ch04: The mistake is treating a feeling as independent evidence. Often it is the end of a cue chain, so the better move is to trace what activated the judgment before trusting it.

thinking-fast-and-slow-ch05: Most readers assume they correct for clear writing: they know a legible memo is easier to read and believe they factor that out. They do not. Fluency binds silently to judgments of truth, competence, and character, and knowing the effect exists barely dents it.

thinking-fast-and-slow-ch06: Surprise does not just make you curious. It pressures the mind to restore order with a cause, so the better move is to separate the broken expectation from the story you are tempted to invent.

thinking-fast-and-slow-ch07: The trap is not speed alone. A thin story can feel complete because WYSIATI treats visible evidence as enough, so the better move is to ask what is absent before confidence hardens.

thinking-fast-and-slow-ch08: Quick judgment is not just emotion. The mind often answers a hard, vague question by matching intensity on an easier scale, so the better move is to identify that hidden scale.

thinking-fast-and-slow-ch09: The substitution is usually not deliberate evasion. The mind keeps moving by answering an easier proxy question, then fails to notice the target question was never answered.

thinking-fast-and-slow-ch10: The mistake is not using small samples at all. The mistake is treating their neatness as stability, when random fluctuation can look representative long before the sample size deserves confidence.
thinking-fast-and-slow-ch11: The anchor does not need to be relevant or fair. A starting point can pull judgment even when everyone knows it is only a number in the room.

thinking-fast-and-slow-ch12: The mistake is not noticing memorable examples. The mistake is treating ease of recall as frequency, when memory fluency often measures salience rather than base occurrence.
thinking-fast-and-slow-ch13: The better move is not to ignore fear. Name the vivid image or feeling that enlarged the risk, then measure frequency, exposure, and severity separately.

thinking-fast-and-slow-ch14: The vivid profile may be diagnostic, but it is not allowed to erase the base rate. The better move is to put the category frequencies back on the table before sorting the case.
thinking-fast-and-slow-ch15: The richer story can be less likely. When added detail makes an option more plausible but mathematically narrower, prefer the broader category first.
thinking-fast-and-slow-ch16: The problem is not that stories are false and statistics are pure. The problem is when a causal story replaces the distribution it was meant to update.
thinking-fast-and-slow-ch17: A rebound after an extreme result does not prove praise worked or blame failed. Often it is regression to the mean: random variation moving back toward average.
thinking-fast-and-slow-ch18: The better move is not to throw intuition away. Use it as evidence, then shrink the forecast toward the base rate when the signal is noisy or correlation is weak.
thinking-fast-and-slow-ch19: The error is not believing every success story. The error is letting a smooth story erase the rivals, accidents, and weak signals that made the outcome uncertain.

thinking-fast-and-slow-ch20: Confidence is not always ego. Often it is the feeling of a coherent story forming, even when the environment gives weak feedback about whether that story predicts anything.

thinking-fast-and-slow-ch21: A formula is not magic, and expertise is not useless. In stable prediction tasks, a simple consistent rule can beat judgment because it removes noise that nuance keeps reintroducing.

thinking-fast-and-slow-ch22: The right test is not credentials versus skepticism. Trust intuition when the environment is regular and feedback has trained the pattern; withhold trust when either condition is missing.
thinking-fast-and-slow-ch23: The outside view is not pessimism. It is the discipline of starting with comparable completed cases before your own details persuade you that this time is different.

thinking-fast-and-slow-ch24: Optimism is not simply foolish or heroic. It creates action, persistence, and enterprise, but it must be forced through survival odds, competition, and a premortem before money or trust is exposed.
thinking-fast-and-slow-ch25: The mistake is not bad arithmetic. It is evaluating choices only by final wealth when people actually feel gains and losses from a reference point.

thinking-fast-and-slow-ch26: The better move is not to label every caution as risk aversion. Read the reference point, the steeper pain of loss, and the way small and certain probabilities get overweighted.
thinking-fast-and-slow-ch27: The endowment effect is not only greed or nostalgia. Ownership turns giving something up into a loss, so the selling price can jump above the buying price.
thinking-fast-and-slow-ch28: The correction is not pessimism. It is recognizing asymmetry: bad events seize attention, motivation, and memory more fiercely than equal good events.
thinking-fast-and-slow-ch29: People are not simply risk-averse or risk-seeking. Their appetite flips when the outcome is a gain or loss, and when the probability is high or low.
thinking-fast-and-slow-ch30: Rare events are not always exaggerated or always ignored. Descriptions can make them loom, while experience can make them fade until the rare outcome finally appears.
thinking-fast-and-slow-ch31: The fix is not to become braver about risk. It is to stop deciding each bet in isolation and use a standing policy that sees the whole portfolio.

thinking-fast-and-slow-ch32: Mental accounting is not ordinary budgeting. It is the habit of putting outcomes into separate ledgers that can make sunk costs, paper losses, and account closure drive the next choice.

thinking-fast-and-slow-ch33: A preference reversal is not just hypocrisy. The evaluation mode changes salience: single evaluation highlights one attribute, while joint evaluation makes comparison easier.
thinking-fast-and-slow-ch34: Framing is not mere spin. Equivalent descriptions can make the same reality feel like a gain or a loss, and those feelings change decisions.
thinking-fast-and-slow-ch35: This is not a split personality story. The experiencing self lives the moments; the remembering self later evaluates the episode and can overrule duration.
thinking-fast-and-slow-ch36: The point is not that memory is fake. It is compressed: remembered utility often overweights peaks and endings while underweighting duration.
thinking-fast-and-slow-ch37: Well-being is not only a global life rating. To understand it, sample lived time: what people are doing, feeling, and enduring while the minutes happen.
thinking-fast-and-slow-ch38: Life satisfaction is not a pure reading of life. The judgment can be pulled by whatever attention has made salient: money, weather, health, status, memory, or meaning.

usedQuizExplanationFrames: thinking-fast-and-slow-ch01:q01: The calm appearance is a System 1 proposal, not a checked judgment. Verifying the potassium value lets System 2 endorse or revise the impression. Arrival order avoids one shortcut by replacing it with a rule unrelated to clinical risk.

thinking-fast-and-slow-ch01:q02: The issue is the handoff: a fast social read is acting as the verdict before the work sample is checked. The second choice overpraises slow thought, and the third throws away useful recognition rather than testing it.

thinking-fast-and-slow-ch01:q03: The eye may be right, but the posted note is exactly the evidence System 2 must check before endorsement. Sending the plate back trusts arrival speed. Asking the chef silently leaves the same hidden sequence intact.

thinking-fast-and-slow-ch01:q04: The green dashboard supplies a fast proposal. The risk-register check is the deliberate endorsement step. Trusting the color confuses cue with proof, while waiting for no uncertainty is an impossible standard.

thinking-fast-and-slow-ch01:q05: The label can trigger a valuable System 1 suspicion, but the pigment test is the endorsement check. Ignoring the label rejects a useful cue; making the test conditional on readability misses the evidence problem.

thinking-fast-and-slow-ch01:q06: System 2 has found evidence that changes the initial social read, so endorsement should be revised. Trusting the impression ignores the check. Averaging without sequence hides the exact correction this move requires.

thinking-fast-and-slow-ch01:q07: The point is the relationship between proposal and endorsement. Forecast pattern recognition may be skilled, but contrary upper-air data must be checked. The other choices turn the idea into blanket distrust or delay.

thinking-fast-and-slow-ch01:q08: Stating the hypothesis keeps System 1 visible while the records give System 2 something concrete to endorse. Searching only for support protects the first answer. Releasing immediately makes the opposite unchecked leap.

thinking-fast-and-slow-ch01:q09: The sentence preserves both roles: fast proposal and slower checking. The second choice describes rationalization, not review. The third turns functional labels into a personality split, which is the wrong frame.

thinking-fast-and-slow-ch02:q01: The familiar label is easy to process, but the dose check needs scarce attention now. Waiting until later misses the moment of risk. Quick recognition may help, but it cannot replace the weight and indication comparison.

thinking-fast-and-slow-ch02:q02: The visual read saves effort, but the real call requires mental work with measurements. Delay cost matters, yet a closed wall is costlier if wrong. A vote spreads opinion, not necessarily attention to the needed comparison.

thinking-fast-and-slow-ch02:q03: The calm report may be accurate, but its fluency can dominate a capacity-heavy decision. The issue is not voice quality or radio distrust. The issue is whether attention has carried all relevant variables before endorsement.

thinking-fast-and-slow-ch02:q04: The glossy cue lowers effort and feels like sellability. Checking stock and last sale date spends attention on the actual constraint. Trusting taste skips the needed data; refusing all glossy books turns a warning into a crude rule.

thinking-fast-and-slow-ch02:q05: The sonar cue may contain signal, but the correction required capacity for delayed evidence. Calling the cue useless overcorrects. Memorizing more cues helps only if exceptions still receive attention when they appear.

thinking-fast-and-slow-ch02:q06: The point is capacity, not virtue. Care may motivate a check, but it does not create unlimited attention under load. Procedures matter because they protect the specific mental work a fluent answer would otherwise skip.

thinking-fast-and-slow-ch02:q07: The alarm captures attention, but the fan decision depends on a comparison that needs mental work. The group chat can amplify the same cue. The cross-block data check directs attention to the variables that decide cost and risk.

thinking-fast-and-slow-ch02:q08: The dense table is the effortful part that controls the outcome. The summary may help orient the adjuster, but trusting it first lets ease replace capacity. Skipping every tired file is too broad; the needed step is protected attention.

thinking-fast-and-slow-ch02:q09: Interruptions tax the capacity needed to compare labels, so effortful checking weakens despite motivation. Carelessness blames character. Label design may matter, but the load pattern points directly to attention being spent elsewhere.

thinking-fast-and-slow-ch03:q01: The three cues make an easy answer, but the exact suffix is the cheap audit. Asking the passenger adds another impression. The lazy controller is caught by making endorsement wait for the identifier.

thinking-fast-and-slow-ch03:q02: The close times create a convenient answer, but endorsement should wait for product and window checks. The other choices overreach: efficiency and human judgment can be useful when the relevant constraints are monitored.

thinking-fast-and-slow-ch06:q01: The unusual refund is a real surprise, but fraud is only one cause. Checking dependent status and withholding tests the explanation. Marking fraud skips the separation; ignoring the refund drops the useful signal.

thinking-fast-and-slow-ch06:q04: The loose strap violates a preservation norm, but mishandling is only one cause. The environmental and handling checks distinguish mechanisms. Avoiding investigation is as weak as blaming too fast.

thinking-fast-and-slow-ch06:q06: The timing is vivid, but electrical checks are what connect flicker to mechanism. Removing the client may help testing but does not replace the checks. Accepting the timing turns coincidence into cause.

thinking-fast-and-slow-ch06:q07: Experience can offer a candidate cause, but surprise also pressures premature closure. Testing the cause against alternatives preserves experience without letting it skip evidence. The other choices either reject or freeze the signal.

thinking-fast-and-slow-ch06:q08: The one-word reply breaks a communication norm, but anger is only one cause. Time pressure, mobile typing, or simple agreement may explain it. Ignoring the message avoids the cause question rather than improving it.

thinking-fast-and-slow-ch06:q09: The spike is the violation; campaign is only one cause. Testing several explanations avoids the first repair story. Assuming the calendar is wrong protects the first cause, while restarting may erase evidence before diagnosis.

thinking-fast-and-slow-ch07:q01: The visible pattern matters, but WYSIATI hides the absent buoy. Checking or substituting that measurement tests the story. Ignoring the pattern overcorrects; issuing the forecast treats coherence as completeness.

thinking-fast-and-slow-ch07:q04: The visible cues fit a low-risk story, but missing history can matter. The other choices make false clinical claims. The actual issue is confidence from thin evidence.

thinking-fast-and-slow-ch07:q05: Writing the story keeps it visible while missing process facts test it. Accepting the story trusts coherence. Avoiding cause gives up on evidence instead of widening the field.

thinking-fast-and-slow-ch07:q06: Concern is justified, but the verdict is incomplete without facts that directly affect attendance. Ignoring visible negatives is as sloppy as treating them as the whole person.

thinking-fast-and-slow-ch07:q07: The flaw is confusing coherence with completeness. Large datasets and total avoidance of confidence are not the lesson. The key is asking what missing evidence would matter.

thinking-fast-and-slow-ch07:q08: The interview story may be useful, but missing evidence outside the story can matter more. Advancing confuses coherence with coverage. Rejecting polish creates the opposite unsupported conclusion.

thinking-fast-and-slow-ch07:q09: The complaints are visible and coherent, but without exposure or usage logs their rate is unknown. The answer is not to ignore complaints or privilege them over records; it is to ask what is absent.

thinking-fast-and-slow-ch08:q01: The messy signature may matter, but only through a defined scale. Naming ID, timing, dose, and prescriber prevents visual disorder from answering the whole legitimacy question. Ignoring or trusting the signature both skip the scale check.

thinking-fast-and-slow-ch08:q03: The dark mark supplies intensity, but the evacuation scale is operational. The largest zone may be needed in some cases, but the decision should come from spread, exits, wind, and occupancy, not visual force alone.

thinking-fast-and-slow-ch08:q08: Emotional intensity may be information, but it is not the same scale as clinical urgency. Formal criteria keep vividness from over-answering the question. Downgrading vivid complaints makes the inverse error.

thinking-fast-and-slow-ch09:q01: The agent answered a trustworthiness proxy, not the ownership target question. Ownership needs tag, flight, and contents evidence. Airline responsibility is a separate issue and would not justify release either.

thinking-fast-and-slow-ch09:q05: Calmness is an accessible proxy for stability, but medical risk needs injury, breathing, fall height, and feeding facts. The other swaps do not match the evidence described.

thinking-fast-and-slow-ch09:q08: Affect toward the specialist is a proxy, not the safety answer. Complication rates, patient factors, and context address the target. Avoiding recommendation because a feeling appeared is too broad.

thinking-fast-and-slow-ch09:q09: Substitution is exposed by comparing the target question with the answered heuristic question. Ease and confidence may be clues, but they do not reveal the swap by themselves.

thinking-fast-and-slow-ch10:q01: Three clean dives matter, but the sample is too small for a stable route claim. Ignoring them throws away useful warning or reassurance; declaring safety treats sampling noise as proof.

thinking-fast-and-slow-ch10:q02: The early rate is interesting, not decisive. Wider comparisons test whether it is signal or sampling noise. Immediate shift overtrusts the tiny count, while ten years is an absurd standard.

thinking-fast-and-slow-ch10:q03: The failures warrant caution, but two cases can reflect variance, handling, rind thickness, or timing. Permanent shutdown treats the small sample as settled; ignoring it underreacts.

thinking-fast-and-slow-ch10:q06: Two disputed calls can be random fluctuation without a denominator. Firsthand experience may contain signal, but the stable-trait claim needs comparison. Punishment is premature without pattern evidence.

thinking-fast-and-slow-ch10:q07: The correction is calibrated: small samples are signals with high noise, not garbage and not proof. Ignoring complaints and declaring a trend both mishandle sampling noise.
thinking-fast-and-slow-ch10:q08: The new script may be bad, but two no-shows must be read against baseline variance and a bigger sample. Abandoning overreacts; keeping forever refuses to learn.

thinking-fast-and-slow-ch10:q09: Three wins may be noise, seasonality, or prospect mix. A larger comparison with prior conversion tests the claim. Confidence and liking are possible side details, not evidence that the email caused the streak.

thinking-fast-and-slow-ch11:q01: Moving down from 900,000 may still be insufficient adjustment. A component estimate creates a separate starting point. Rejecting all awards overreacts to the anchor instead of correcting it.

thinking-fast-and-slow-ch11:q02: The old reading can anchor the estimate even if it contains some information. The correction is not to ban prior values, but to build today's reading from current calibration and sample evidence first.

thinking-fast-and-slow-ch11:q03: The repair estimate should come from work components, not from adjustment around 45. Doubling is arbitrary and still anchor-driven. A small downward adjustment may feel careful while staying too close.

thinking-fast-and-slow-ch11:q05: Fourteen feels conservative only relative to 18. Component evidence points to nine. The night estimate may be useful context later, but it should not set the starting point.

thinking-fast-and-slow-ch11:q07: The bed estimate shows anchoring in operational forecasting, not bargaining. The other examples are price negotiation and do not refute the narrow view.

thinking-fast-and-slow-ch11:q08: The changed format means the anchor may be a poor starting point. Building from current drivers prevents insufficient adjustment. Inflation is another adjustment around the old number.

thinking-fast-and-slow-ch11:q09: An independent estimate creates a clean starting point. Prior numbers can be useful later, so permanent ignorance is too broad. Averaging anchored estimates can simply average the bias.

thinking-fast-and-slow-ch12:q01: The vivid memory is a cue, not a rate. Checking similar refunds supplies base occurrence. Strong flagging overuses salience; ignoring the memory misses a useful hypothesis.
thinking-fast-and-slow-ch12:q02: Frequency requires a numerator and denominator. Customer anger explains salience, not occurrence. Weekday may be a clue only after the base rate is known.

thinking-fast-and-slow-ch12:q03: The fatal slide deserves attention, but memory fluency can overstate frequency. Similar-slope counts and pit results provide the rate. Ignoring or permanently equalizing risk both mishandle salience.
thinking-fast-and-slow-ch12:q04: Policy needs base occurrence across handling, not story frequency in staff chat. Apology may matter for one case, but it does not answer how common mishandling is.

thinking-fast-and-slow-ch12:q05: The photo increases memory fluency, not necessarily occurrence. Counts can still miss severity, but frequency is not established by image salience. Ignoring the defect would miss a possible severity issue.

thinking-fast-and-slow-ch12:q06: Availability supplies a hypothesis, not the rate. Repair counts and readings distinguish likely causes. Treating the memory as proof or banning it entirely both skip the base occurrence check.

thinking-fast-and-slow-ch12:q07: The customer photo shows memory fluency created inside work, without media. News can create availability too, but it is not the whole mechanism. Dramatic wording is only one salience source.

thinking-fast-and-slow-ch12:q08: Risk ranking needs event count and exposure. Severity may justify immediate safeguards, but frequency still needs a denominator. Dropping the issue ignores a serious signal.

thinking-fast-and-slow-ch12:q09: The complaints may reveal a real issue, but frequency requires counts. Treating anecdotes as the whole truth overuses availability; ignoring them loses qualitative signal.

thinking-fast-and-slow-ch13:q01: The footage may signal what people fear, but current risk needs measurement. Ignoring it loses situational awareness; escalating from the image alone lets availability drive risk perception.

thinking-fast-and-slow-ch13:q02: The outside outbreak made the risk emotionally available. Local readings still matter. Caring about mold is appropriate; matching public concern without local evidence overreacts.

thinking-fast-and-slow-ch13:q03: The image identifies a possible hazard but not its frequency in this case. Comparable records and route facts calibrate risk. Fear is a signal to inspect, not a risk model.

thinking-fast-and-slow-ch13:q05: The photo makes risk vivid, but temperature, holding time, and batch history answer the actual safety question. Concern is appropriate; skipping controls is the error.

thinking-fast-and-slow-ch13:q06: Appearance risk needs case-level factors. Office fear shows the availability cascade, not the client's probability. The client's awareness of the story does not answer the risk estimate.

thinking-fast-and-slow-ch13:q07: The balanced move is to name fear and then measure. Treating fear as reliable overweights emotion; rejecting numbers when emotion is strong gives the cascade full control.

thinking-fast-and-slow-ch13:q08: Policy should respect concern but calibrate by risk measures. The video alone may distort priorities. Ignoring public concern entirely can miss trust and communication needs.

thinking-fast-and-slow-ch13:q09: The video may reveal a serious scenario, but broad change should follow frequency, exposure, and severity checks. Parent fear matters for communication, not as a substitute for risk evidence.

thinking-fast-and-slow-ch14:q01: The profile may carry signal, but the low base rate matters first. Strong flagging lets stereotype fit replace probability. Ignoring the profile loses potentially diagnostic details.

thinking-fast-and-slow-ch14:q02: The notes fit a specialty image, but the roster base rate resists that conclusion. The other choices treat style as more diagnostic than category frequency and credentials.

thinking-fast-and-slow-ch14:q03: The calm voice updates the estimate only if it is diagnostic. Records answer whether expertise exists. Assuming either way without records mishandles the base rate and description.

thinking-fast-and-slow-ch14:q04: Performance data are more diagnostic of skill than resemblance to a prototype. Communication style can inform coaching, but it should not override base performance evidence.

thinking-fast-and-slow-ch14:q05: The offer should start with category frequency and diagnostic book details. The seller's style creates representativeness, but it is weaker than edition, condition, provenance, and sales evidence.

thinking-fast-and-slow-ch14:q06: The profile resembles a risk category, but the block base rate and leaf temperature are essential. Ignoring the profile loses useful information; trusting it alone lets representativeness dominate.

thinking-fast-and-slow-ch14:q09: A vivid match to a rare condition should prompt targeted checking, not immediate diagnosis. The base rate keeps common causes on the table while diagnostic signs are tested.

thinking-fast-and-slow-ch15:q01: Ownership contains the detailed ownership-plus-violinist story. The detail may aid verification, but it cannot make the narrower event more probable than the broad category.

thinking-fast-and-slow-ch15:q03: The broader transit-delay category includes the narrower reeds story. Vividness increases plausibility, not probability. Evidence for reeds can be added later.

thinking-fast-and-slow-ch15:q06: The broad slip category includes the slip-plus-refund story. The refund may become plausible with evidence, but probability falls when conditions are added.

thinking-fast-and-slow-ch15:q07: The containment check exposes when a detailed conjunction is being ranked above its broader category. Details can be diagnostic, but they cannot make a subset more probable than its superset.

thinking-fast-and-slow-ch15:q08: Churn alone is broader than churn plus public complaint. The angry ticket may raise both estimates, but the combined event cannot outrank the broader one on probability.
thinking-fast-and-slow-ch15:q09: Containment identifies the broader category. Interesting and familiar stories can increase plausibility while lowering probability if they add conditions.

thinking-fast-and-slow-ch16:q01: The deckhand story may be true, but it must update the route distribution rather than replace it. Ignoring the failure underreacts; accepting the story overtrusts causality without evidence.

thinking-fast-and-slow-ch16:q02: The school story explains the essay but may overrule a strong distribution. Essays and reputation can update the rate, but neither should erase comparable applicant outcomes.

thinking-fast-and-slow-ch16:q03: The explanation is actionable only if it updates the defect distribution. Immediate blame lets the story replace the chart. Waiting a full year is unnecessary if current logs can test the cause.

thinking-fast-and-slow-ch16:q05: The technician may be involved, but adjustment rates and case complexity must test that cause. Removing the technician or dismissing rates lets the story outrun evidence.
thinking-fast-and-slow-ch16:q06: The causal story needs support from the distribution of calls. A balanced record does not prove no bias, but it weakens that particular explanation.
thinking-fast-and-slow-ch16:q07: The balanced move keeps both: distributions set the base, causal evidence updates it. Removing stories loses mechanisms; dismissing statistics loses calibration.

thinking-fast-and-slow-ch16:q08: The receptionist story may be testable, but it should update rates only if evidence changes. Ignoring complaints misses qualitative signal; disciplining jumps from story to action.
thinking-fast-and-slow-ch16:q09: The restart question puts the base rate or distribution back in view. Story quality and accountability may matter later, but they do not calibrate risk.

thinking-fast-and-slow-ch17:q01: The bad session may have been an extreme outcome followed by regression. Coaching can help, but the rebound alone is not proof. Tone of coaching is weaker than comparison with baseline.

thinking-fast-and-slow-ch17:q02: The filter may have helped, but a high reading often moves back toward average. Repeated readings and usual variance are needed. Ignoring the spike or dismissing fixes both overreach.
thinking-fast-and-slow-ch17:q03: The 12-minute repair was extreme relative to the 45-minute average. A 42-minute repair looks ordinary, not necessarily complacent. Praise may have had no causal role.
thinking-fast-and-slow-ch17:q04: A 98 may be an extreme outcome with luck. The 87 may be ordinary for the garden. Mood and confidence do not test regression against the average.
thinking-fast-and-slow-ch17:q05: The 19-day is near the average, while 34 is extreme. Regression explains part of the rebound. Blame and abandonment require more evidence than two days.

thinking-fast-and-slow-ch17:q06: The standout scene may include favorable source footage and luck. Ordinary later scenes should be compared with average work before judging talent. Praise alone does not explain the return.

thinking-fast-and-slow-ch17:q07: Regression is about movement toward average after extremity. It can follow high or low results. It does not deny talent; it separates talent from luck and random variation.

thinking-fast-and-slow-ch17:q08: A comparison helps separate intervention effect from regression. Intensity of criticism does not prove causality. The worse the month, the more regression alone could explain a rebound.
thinking-fast-and-slow-ch17:q09: The report should keep both possibilities open. An extreme low is likely to rebound somewhat. More runs can show whether the checklist changed the average.
thinking-fast-and-slow-ch18:q01: The cues should update the base rate, not replace it. Ignoring them underuses evidence; jumping to the gut forecast overuses noisy case impressions.
thinking-fast-and-slow-ch18:q02: The smell is a cue with imperfect correlation. The forecast should rise but shrink toward the base rate. Zero and 90 both ignore calibration.
thinking-fast-and-slow-ch18:q03: The crack matters, but correlation and comparable conditions decide how far to move the forecast. Fear and arbitrary low anchors both mishandle the cue.
thinking-fast-and-slow-ch18:q04: Moderate correlation means the letter should move the forecast, but not all the way to the intuitive high value. Ignoring it and overreacting both misweight evidence.
thinking-fast-and-slow-ch18:q05: The defect is informative but noisy. A shrunken forecast respects both base rate and signal. The other choices treat the cue as either destiny or nothing.
thinking-fast-and-slow-ch18:q06: The frost resemblance is a cue, not a final diagnosis. Base rates and checks determine how much to shift. Dismissing frost outright ignores a possible signal.
thinking-fast-and-slow-ch18:q07: The method combines intuition with base rates and shrinkage. Banning intuition loses signal; ignoring base rates loses calibration.

thinking-fast-and-slow-ch18:q08: A brilliant interview is positive evidence, but moderate correlation means the forecast should be tempered. The correct estimate sits between base rate and first impression.

thinking-fast-and-slow-ch18:q09: Unknown reliability should not give intuition unlimited weight. Shrinking toward the base rate protects against noisy cues. Refusing every forecast is usually impractical.
thinking-fast-and-slow-ch19:q01: The result is useful evidence, but it should not erase rival paths or luck. The wrong success story overclaims; rejecting all causes throws away real learning.
thinking-fast-and-slow-ch19:q02: The correction restores real-time uncertainty. The recovery may teach something, but only after separating available evidence from hindsight glow.
thinking-fast-and-slow-ch19:q03: The causes may be partly real, but the smooth chain overstates predictability. The tempting wrong answers turn healthy doubt into blanket rejection.
thinking-fast-and-slow-ch19:q04: Real-time knowledge is the anchor. Quick blame lets coherence replace evidence, while ignoring the delay refuses to learn from the outcome.
thinking-fast-and-slow-ch19:q05: The best move checks the later story against earlier live risks. The palette may matter, but making it the sole cause is coherence masquerading as proof.

thinking-fast-and-slow-ch19:q08: The menu may be part of the story, but the review should restore other plausible causes. Choosing the cleanest cause confuses fluency with accuracy.
thinking-fast-and-slow-ch19:q09: The team has a story; the problem is that it is too complete after the failure. The logistical alternatives keep judgment tied to what was actually knowable.
thinking-fast-and-slow-ch20:q01: The coherent cue deserves attention, but the outcome record limits confidence. Ignoring the cue loses safety; full certainty mistakes fit for validity.
thinking-fast-and-slow-ch20:q02: Weak feedback means the confidence needs a discount. The cues may still matter, but they have not earned the certainty the coherent story creates.
thinking-fast-and-slow-ch20:q03: Action and confidence are separate. Urgency may require action, but weak verification should reduce stated certainty rather than inflate it.
thinking-fast-and-slow-ch20:q04: Selected feedback shows only part of the comparison set. It can make confidence feel trained while hiding missed opportunities and false negatives.
thinking-fast-and-slow-ch20:q05: Coherence explains the confidence, not the accuracy. Verified feedback is the test that the clean story failed.
thinking-fast-and-slow-ch20:q06: The remembered cases are selected. Full feedback, including misses and false alarms, decides whether the cue predicts frost.
thinking-fast-and-slow-ch20:q07: The interview can inform the choice, but weak validity limits confidence. The tempting errors either demonize fluency or let it override the record.
thinking-fast-and-slow-ch20:q08: Without outcome feedback, confidence cannot be trained. More crisp language increases coherence, while banning narrative misses the validity problem.
thinking-fast-and-slow-ch20:q09: Cue coherence can generate confidence before accuracy is known. Predictive validity depends on whether that judgment type succeeds against outcomes.
thinking-fast-and-slow-ch21:q01: The task is repeated and stable enough for a rule to reduce noise. Passenger emotion may matter for service, but it should not replace proven predictors.
thinking-fast-and-slow-ch21:q02: The formula gets first weight in a stable prediction task. Expertise can override only with specific evidence, not with status or a vivid story.
thinking-fast-and-slow-ch21:q03: The formula is useful because it reduces noisy overreaction to one scene. It does not guarantee perfection or eliminate expert listening.
thinking-fast-and-slow-ch21:q04: The score protects a repeated decision from social pressure and call noise. Splitting crews ignores the priority signal; call volume alone can mislead.

thinking-fast-and-slow-ch22:q01: The warning has a credible learning history. Seniority alone is not enough, but repeated similar cases with clear feedback can produce skill.
